verdictExplanation: The assistant reviews business contracts that contain names and contact details, and sends them to a US-hosted model. That likely triggers BC PIPA purpose and consent duties and PIPEDA accountability for information sent to the vendor, with OPC draft vendor guidance to consider. These are conditions to plan for, not blockers, and Bill C-36 is shown only as something to prepare for.

intake.title: Equipment-lease contract clause review
intake.processDescription: Our legal team reviews incoming equipment-lease contracts from business customers. A paralegal reads each contract, compares the clauses with our clause playbook, flags non-standard terms and drafts a redline for a lawyer, who decides which positions to take. Contracts contain the names and contact details of customer representatives and guarantors. We want a large language model to extract clauses, compare them with the playbook, recommend a position on non-standard clauses and draft redline suggestions.

subtasks.name: Extract clauses from incoming contracts
subtasks.description: The AI reads each incoming equipment-lease contract and pulls out the key clauses and the party details so they can be compared with the playbook.
subtasks.rationale: Extraction follows clear patterns and errors are caught in later review. Contracts name representatives and guarantors, so personal details are involved.

subtasks.name: Compare clauses with the clause playbook
subtasks.description: Each extracted clause is checked against the clause playbook to see whether it matches the standard position or differs from it.
subtasks.rationale: The playbook is written down, but matching wording to a standard needs some weighing. A missed difference could pass to the lawyer, so errors cause rework or delay.

subtasks.name: Flag non-standard terms
subtasks.description: Clauses that differ from the playbook, or are missing, are marked as non-standard so the lawyer can focus on them.
subtasks.rationale: Deciding what counts as non-standard draws on experience. A missed flag could lead to unfavourable terms being accepted, which is a costly business error.

subtasks.name: Recommend a position on non-standard clauses
subtasks.description: For each non-standard clause, the AI suggests a position our side could take, for the lawyer to accept, change or reject.
subtasks.rationale: Weighing risk against commercial aims is a matter on which experienced lawyers can disagree. A poor recommendation could shape contract terms. Only businesses are affected.

subtasks.name: Draft redline suggestions
subtasks.description: The AI drafts proposed edits to the contract wording, reflecting the recommended positions, for a lawyer to review.
subtasks.rationale: Drafting wording takes skill that is hard to write down. Errors that slip through could put poor terms in a contract, but the lawyer reviews the draft.

subtasks.name: Decide which positions to take
subtasks.description: A lawyer reviews the flagged clauses, recommendations and redlines, and decides which positions to take with the customer.
subtasks.rationale: This is the final judgment, weighing legal risk and business aims. A wrong call has costly effects, though it concerns business terms rather than a person's rights.

assumptions: A lawyer reviews every redline before it goes to the customer.
The clause playbook is a written document that the AI can be given.
Guarantors are named in the contract but are not the subject of any decision in this process.
Contracts are in a digital, readable format.
The AI output is a recommendation only and the lawyer makes the final decision.
clarifyingQuestions: Are guarantors assessed or decided on in this process, or only named in contracts?
How often do contracts depart from the playbook, and how is that tracked?
Does the lawyer review every clause or only the ones flagged?
